contexts.title: Section 102: money for Homeland Security Investigations
contexts.html: Section 102 gives Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) $7.45 billion, available until September 30, 2029, “to hire, pay, train, and equip Homeland Security Investigations agents and support personnel”. Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) is the part of ICE that investigates crimes. The money “shall be used for functions other than those related to Homeland Security Investigations' immigration enforcement and customs enforcement missions”. Section 102 also requires that $108.5 million be used for added child exploitation investigators and analysts, “to support the identification and rescue of victims of child sexual exploitation and abuse”.

contexts.title: Sections 101 and 103: Border Patrol duties other than immigration, aircraft, boats and equipment
contexts.html: Section 101 gives Customs and Border Protection (CBP) $9.55 billion, available until September 30, 2029, “to hire, pay, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and Border Patrol support personnel to conduct functions other than immigration enforcement and customs functions”. Section 103 pays for “Air and Marine operations' upgrading and procurement of new platforms for rapid air and marine response capabilities”, for new inspection equipment “to combat the entry or exit of illicit narcotics at ports of entry and along the southwest, northern, and maritime borders”, for “combating drug trafficking, including fentanyl and its precursor chemicals”, and for border surveillance technology. Tower money may not go to towers that “have not been tested and accepted by U.S. Customs and Border Protection to deliver autonomous capabilities.”

contexts.title: Section 202: ICE staff, removal, facilities, lawyers and 287(g) agreements
contexts.html: Section 202 gives ICE $31.075 billion for immigration enforcement. It covers “Hiring, paying, training, and equipping U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement personnel and the personnel for all its directorates”; “Funding for transportation costs and related costs associated with alien departure or removal operations”; “fleet maintenance and sustainment” and “operations and maintenance for its immigration enforcement functions”; government attorneys “to represent the Department in immigration enforcement and removal proceedings”; and “Supporting coordination with state and local authorities by expanding, facilitating, and implementing agreements under section 287(g)”. A 287(g) agreement lets trained state or local police do some immigration enforcement work, inside jails, during routine police work, or by serving warrants on people in custody. At least $350 million is set aside for arrests and custody work in places that do not meet the bill’s cooperation rules, and “None of the funds appropriated pursuant to this paragraph may be used, except as required by existing law, to release, parole, place on alternatives to detention”.

Unspent money does not by itself show that S.2 adds nothing.

nodes.title: Fewer crossings through some wild areas
nodes.claim_html: Border staff and surveillance paid for by S.2 would reduce, and not only move, unlawful crossings through at least some wild areas near the border.

nodes.title: Less trash fouling water that wildlife uses
nodes.claim_html: Fewer crossings through those wild areas would mean less trash left near water sources, so less of that water would be fouled for wildlife.

nodes.title: Less spread of invasive species
nodes.claim_html: Fewer crossings through parks and refuges would reduce one way that invasive species spread there.

nodes.title: Fewer wildfires from abandoned campfires
nodes.claim_html: Fewer crossings through fire-prone wild land would mean fewer abandoned warming and cooking fires, and so fewer wildfires started that way.

nodes.title: Less trail and fence damage from faster detection
nodes.claim_html: Autonomous towers paid for by S.2 would lead to faster catching of people crossing, and this would reduce damaging trails and broken habitat fences, not only shorten response times.

nodes.title: Earlier fire warnings and calls for help
nodes.claim_html: Border Patrol staff paid for by Section 101 would add at least some early fire warnings and calls for firefighting help, helping crews control fires in natural areas.

nodes.title: More illegal fishing stopped
nodes.claim_html: Aircraft and boats paid for by Section 103 would help stop at least some more illegal fishing that harms sea life.

nodes.title: Added help coordinating oil-spill cleanup
nodes.claim_html: Aircraft paid for by Section 103 would add to CBP’s occasional ability to help coordinate oil-spill cleanup.

nodes.title: Nature: less damage to land, water and sea life
nodes.claim_html: Less fouled wildlife water, less trail and fence damage, less spread of invasive species, fewer wildfires, faster-controlled fires, less illegal fishing and more occasional ability to help coordinate oil-spill cleanup each protect plants, wildlife, soil or water from destruction and pollution. That serves caring for nature. Each needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: Land officers’ time kept for conservation
nodes.claim_html: S.2’s added border staff would take on more border enforcement work on public lands, leaving land officers more time to protect natural resources.

nodes.title: Planned burns made easier
nodes.claim_html: Border Patrol staff paid for by Section 101 would help make planned-burn work areas safe, so that land managers can carry out more of these burns.

nodes.title: Nature: conservation work supported
nodes.claim_html: Land officers’ time for resource protection and planned burns that care for plants are both active conservation work. Supporting that work serves the active defense of nature. Each needs its own claim; either is enough.

nodes.title: More removal flights and their pollution
nodes.claim_html: That added immigration enforcement would include at least some added removal flights paid for by Section 202 transport money, adding climate and local air pollution.

nodes.title: More detention-facility and vehicle operation
nodes.claim_html: That added immigration enforcement would keep more detention facilities and enforcement vehicles operating, or operating longer, than without S.2, through Section 202’s facility, fleet and operations money.

nodes.title: Wildlife kept away from facility sites
nodes.claim_html: Added facility operation would keep migratory birds and other wildlife away from at least some facility sites, a small disturbance.

nodes.title: Air pollution from facilities and vehicles
nodes.claim_html: Added facility and vehicle operation would add air pollution from vehicles and emergency generators.

nodes.title: Planned detention centers beyond sewer capacity
nodes.claim_html: S.2’s operating money would make it at least somewhat more likely that planned warehouse detention centers, such as those at Social Circle, Georgia, and Williamsport, Maryland, operate beyond what local water and sewer systems can handle.

nodes.title: More damaging off-road patrol driving
nodes.claim_html: Section 201 staff money would add or keep going at least some off-road patrol driving that damages desert wilderness.

nodes.title: Forest work left without crews
nodes.claim_html: Those added arrests and removals, paid for by Sections 201 and 202, would leave at least some time-sensitive forest work, such as fire clearing or replanting, without crews, risking erosion and habitat loss.

nodes.title: Nature: pollution and damage to wild land and wildlife
nodes.claim_html: Added flight and facility pollution, wildlife kept from sites, sewage overflows into land and water, off-road damage to desert wilderness and forest work left undone each harm the environment or wildlife. Protecting nature from pollution and destruction gives a reason against adding to them. Each needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: More aerial surveillance of environmental defenders
nodes.claim_html: Section 103 aircraft money would add to or upgrade aircraft used to watch people defending the environment, adding at least some risk of discouraging them from taking part.

nodes.title: Nature: people taking part in defending nature
nodes.claim_html: Taking part in defending nature is part of caring for it. An added risk of discouraging people who do so gives a reason against this money.

nodes.title: Added immigration enforcement beyond the law in force
nodes.claim_html: S.2’s immigration enforcement money in Sections 201 and 202 would pay for at least some immigration arrests, detention, removals or enforcement operations beyond those the law in force already funded. This concerns immigration enforcement only, not the separate investigation, rescue, fire-warning or drug-inspection money.

nodes.title: Added HSI time for criminal investigations
nodes.claim_html: Section 102’s general money would add at least some HSI agent and support-staff time for criminal investigations and victim work outside immigration enforcement, under the staff assignment practices reported before June 9, 2026.

nodes.title: Public-facing tactics of 2025–early 2026 continue
nodes.claim_html: At least some of the added enforcement would continue public-facing tactics from the 2025 and early-2026 record, despite the reported shift toward quieter enforcement.

nodes.title: More abused children identified and rescued
nodes.claim_html: The added child exploitation investigators, analysts and trained police paid for by Section 102 would help identify and rescue at least some more children suffering sexual abuse.

nodes.title: More abuse-prevention teaching for families
nodes.claim_html: That added HSI time would keep or grow Project iGuardian’s teaching for children and families about online sexual abuse.

nodes.title: Added HSI time for human trafficking cases
nodes.claim_html: That added HSI time would reach human trafficking investigations.

nodes.title: More trafficking victims found and brought to safety
nodes.claim_html: That added trafficking investigation work would find at least some more people held in forced sex or labor and bring them out of that control and into protection and care.

nodes.title: Added HSI time for victim services
nodes.claim_html: That added HSI time would reach services helping victims in HSI cases explain their accounts and obtain support.

nodes.title: Added HSI time for financial scam cases
nodes.claim_html: That added HSI time would reach investigations of financial scams, including scams against older people.

nodes.title: Added HSI time for criminal human-rights cases
nodes.claim_html: That added HSI time would reach criminal investigations of human-rights violations and war crimes.

nodes.title: More perpetrators of atrocities held responsible
nodes.claim_html: That added human-rights investigation work would lead to at least some more people who committed human-rights violations or war crimes being prosecuted or otherwise held responsible.

nodes.title: Added HSI time for terrorism cases
nodes.claim_html: That added HSI time would reach terrorism investigations.

nodes.title: Added HSI time for cybercrime cases protecting critical services
nodes.claim_html: That added HSI time would reach cybercrime investigations protecting hospitals, utilities, schools and emergency services.

nodes.title: Less violence from people with violent convictions
nodes.claim_html: The added enforcement would include custody or removal of people with violent criminal convictions, and this would reduce, at least somewhat, the risk of violence to U.S. residents.

nodes.title: Concern: protecting people from abuse, exploitation, fraud and violence
nodes.claim_html: More abused children identified and rescued, more abuse-prevention teaching for families, more people freed from forced sex or work, more help for victims in HSI cases, more investigative work against scams, terrorism and cyberattacks on essential services, and less violence from people with violent convictions each add to the protection of vulnerable people, including strangers. That serves concern for the vulnerable and justice for victims. Each needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: Concern: justice for victims of atrocities abroad
nodes.claim_html: Holding people responsible for human-rights violations and war crimes committed abroad serves justice for victims, including people one has never met.

nodes.title: New drug scanners add usable inspections
nodes.claim_html: Section 103 money for inspection equipment would add at least some usable drug scanning, not only more machines, despite the staff, outage and maintenance limits that auditors reported.

nodes.title: Seized drugs lower the supply that reaches people
nodes.claim_html: Drugs seized with S.2’s added resources would lower, at least somewhat, the amount of dangerous drugs reaching people in the United States, even though traffickers can replace seized drugs. This asks about drugs reaching people overall, not how large the drop would be.

nodes.title: Less fentanyl reaching people
nodes.claim_html: The drugs kept out with the new scanners would include fentanyl, so that at least somewhat less fentanyl reaches people in the United States.

nodes.title: More rescues and emergency help for people in danger
nodes.claim_html: Aircraft and boats paid for by Section 103, or Border Patrol staff paid for by Section 101, would add at least some rescues of, or other emergency help for, people in life-threatening danger.

nodes.title: More medical care for people in custody
nodes.claim_html: Section 202’s operations money would add at least some medical, mental-health or dental care for people in immigration custody.

nodes.title: Concern: lives and health of people at risk
nodes.claim_html: Fewer dangerous drugs reaching people at risk of overdose, more rescues of, or emergency help for, people in danger, and more medical care for people who depend on the government in custody each protect lives and health. That serves concern for vulnerable people of any nationality. Each needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: More recorded encounters for review
nodes.claim_html: Section 202’s technology money would add at least some body-camera use, so that more encounters between officers and the public are recorded and can be reviewed.

nodes.title: Concern: fair review of officers’ conduct
nodes.claim_html: Evidence for reviewing disputed encounters serves the just treatment of people facing government power.

nodes.title: Safer work for agency staff
nodes.claim_html: The bill’s training and equipment money would add at least some protective equipment or safety training that makes agency staff safer from injury.

nodes.title: Concern: protecting workers from known job dangers
nodes.claim_html: Protecting workers against known job dangers is part of treating them justly.

nodes.title: More detention of people who pose no safety threat
nodes.claim_html: The added enforcement would hold in custody at least some more people who pose no public safety threat.

nodes.title: Concern: freedom taken from people who pose no threat
nodes.claim_html: Holding more people who pose no safety threat, or ruling out monitored release for the arrest fund, takes away freedom where a less restrictive option might serve. Just treatment gives a reason against paying for that loss of freedom. The first reason needs its claim; the fund rule is in the bill. Either is enough.

nodes.title: Race-based stops continue
nodes.claim_html: At least some of the added enforcement, including through local agreements, would continue stops based on perceived race, ethnicity or national origin of the kind described in the Los Angeles record.

nodes.title: Removal without a fair chance to reach a lawyer
nodes.claim_html: Added government lawyers and removal capacity would increase the number of detained people who face removal without being able to reach a lawyer.

nodes.title: Added risk of warrantless home entries
nodes.claim_html: S.2’s operating money would add to the risk of home entries without a judge’s warrant, by paying for operations in which the paused practice could resume.

nodes.title: More broad collection of information about people
nodes.claim_html: S.2’s surveillance and technology money would add to broad collection of information about Americans and immigrants, without separating people involved in wrongdoing from everyone else.

nodes.title: Concern: just treatment of people facing enforcement
nodes.claim_html: Stops based on perceived race, removal without a fair chance to reach a lawyer, home entry without a judge’s warrant, and broad collection of information without separating wrongdoers from everyone else each treat people unjustly. Just treatment gives a reason against adding to them. Each needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: More people held in dangerous conditions
nodes.claim_html: The added detention would expose at least some more people, including children and sick people, to conditions such as overcrowding, unsafe food and water, and denial of medical care.

nodes.title: Less yearly leverage over conditions and conduct
nodes.claim_html: Compared with the 2025 budget law, whose detention and enforcement money already runs through fiscal year 2029, S.2’s added money through 2029 would further weaken, at least somewhat, Congress’s practical ability to use yearly funding decisions to demand safer detention conditions and safer conduct in enforcement operations.

nodes.title: More children separated from parents
nodes.claim_html: The added arrests, detention and removals would separate at least some more children from parents whose daily care they need.

nodes.title: Large, visible raids and sweeps continue
nodes.claim_html: The added operations would include large, visible raids or sweeps of the kind linked to the cited community disruption, despite the reported change toward quieter enforcement.

nodes.title: Added community disruption from those raids
nodes.claim_html: Those added raids or sweeps would themselves cause at least some more community disruption of the kind seen in Minnesota, such as people afraid to leave home for food or medicine, children kept from school, and workers and small businesses kept from work, despite the reported changes in how operations are run.

nodes.title: Children’s schooling harmed
nodes.claim_html: The added enforcement actions would harm the schooling of at least some children, including U.S.-born children of U.S.-born parents.

nodes.title: Excessive force in public operations continues
nodes.claim_html: At least some of the added public enforcement operations would continue the excessive force described in the 2025 and early-2026 record, including against peaceful protesters, observers and helpers.

nodes.title: Other workers lose jobs and earnings
nodes.claim_html: The added removals would cost at least some other workers jobs or earnings, through less demand for their work.

nodes.title: Concern: harms to vulnerable people from added enforcement
nodes.claim_html: More people held in dangerous conditions, less yearly leverage to demand safer conditions, children separated from parents, added community disruption from large raids, such as people afraid to get food or medicine, harmed schooling, injury or death in operations, and lost jobs and earnings for other families each harm vulnerable people. Protecting them gives a reason against these harms. Each needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: More immigration cases against persecutors
nodes.claim_html: Section 202’s added ICE staff, including investigators and lawyers, would add at least some immigration cases against people who persecuted others for their race, religion, nationality, group or political opinion, so that at least some more of them are removed to face justice or otherwise held to account.

nodes.title: Added HSI time against threats to foreign governments’ critics
nodes.claim_html: That added HSI time would reach investigations of foreign governments’ efforts to threaten and silence their critics in the United States.

nodes.title: Tolerance: protection from persecution and silencing
nodes.claim_html: Holding more persecutors responsible, through criminal human-rights cases or immigration cases, and more investigative work against foreign governments’ threats to their critics both defend people’s ability to differ in identity and views. Acceptance of difference and disagreement gives a reason to support that protection. Each needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: Tolerance: understanding and caring for victims unlike oneself
nodes.claim_html: Helping victims explain their experiences across differences in language and culture, and caring for them whatever their immigration status, puts listening to and accepting people who are different into practice, including when one disagrees with their entry or stay.

nodes.title: More people held where minority worship is blocked
nodes.claim_html: The added detention would hold at least some more people in centers where minority religious practice, such as communal Muslim prayer or religious diets, is blocked.

nodes.title: Tolerance: accepting different ethnic, national and religious groups
nodes.claim_html: Stops based on perceived race, ethnicity or national origin, and detention that blocks minority worship, each treat a group’s difference as grounds for suspicion or exclusion. Accepting different groups gives a reason against adding to them. Each needs its own claim; either is enough.

nodes.title: Established neighbors removed from community life
nodes.claim_html: The added removal money would separate at least some more established community members who pose no threat, including parents and people without convictions, from their families and communities.

nodes.title: Tolerance: accepting established neighbors
nodes.claim_html: More ability to remove established community members who are not threats, or an arrest fund that prefers custody to monitored release, works against accepting different people as neighbors. The first reason needs its claim; the fund rule is in the bill. Either is enough.

nodes.title: More withdrawal from police contact and community life
nodes.claim_html: The expanded 287(g) agreements would lead at least some more Latino residents to avoid contact with police and withdraw from community life.

nodes.title: Tolerance: everyday contact across differences
nodes.claim_html: Fear that keeps neighbors apart is a barrier to listening to and understanding people who are different. That gives a reason against adding to it.

nodes.title: Tolerance: hearing people facing deportation
nodes.claim_html: Directing added legal help to the case for deportation, where people in custody face documented barriers to presenting their own case, works against hearing and understanding them.

nodes.title: Surveillance used to intimidate critics and observers
nodes.claim_html: The added surveillance capacity would be used to make peaceful criticism or observation of immigration enforcement feel personally threatening.

nodes.title: Tolerance: peaceful critics and those who report
nodes.claim_html: Force against peaceful protesters, observers and journalists, and surveillance used to make criticism feel personally threatening, both pressure people to hide disagreement. Accepting people who disagree gives a reason against adding to that pressure. Each needs its own claim; either is enough.

nodes.title: Added HSI work taking poisoned counterfeit pills off sale
nodes.claim_html: That added HSI time would reach investigations of fake pharmacies selling poisoned counterfeit pills, as work outside the excluded customs mission, and take at least some more of these pills off sale.

nodes.title: Border health orders supported
nodes.claim_html: Border Patrol staff paid for by Section 101 would support carrying out the public health orders meant to keep infectious disease such as Ebola from reaching U.S. communities, while those orders apply.

nodes.title: Personal Security: health protected from poisoned drugs and disease
nodes.claim_html: Less fentanyl reaching people, poisoned counterfeit pills taken off sale, and border health orders supported each protect people’s health. Each needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: Arrests moved from public places to jails
nodes.claim_html: The expanded 287(g) partnerships would move at least some immigration arrests from public places into jails, avoiding dangerous public confrontations.

nodes.title: Added HSI time against violent gangs
nodes.claim_html: That added HSI time would reach investigations of violent gangs such as MS-13.

nodes.title: Local partners’ work against violent gangs
nodes.claim_html: Section 203 support for state and local crime prevention would add at least some local work against violent gangs, without depending on added HSI staff.

nodes.title: Less gang violence in communities
nodes.claim_html: That added work against violent gangs, by HSI or by local partners, would stop at least some gang violence against people in U.S. communities.

nodes.title: More screening for security threats
nodes.claim_html: Section 201 agents and equipment would add at least some security screening, such as watchlist checks, before people enter U.S. communities.

nodes.title: Personal Security: safety from violence, terrorism and accidents
nodes.claim_html: Less violence from people with violent convictions, arrests moved out of public places, more people freed from trafficking, less gang violence, more security screening against terrorism, and more rescues or other emergency help each protect people’s personal safety. That serves avoiding danger. Each needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: U.S. citizens held without needed care
nodes.claim_html: Among the added people held, at least some would be U.S. citizens, and some of them would be held without needed medical care.

nodes.title: Less crime reporting and police protection
nodes.claim_html: The expanded 287(g) local police role would make at least some victims and witnesses less willing to report crimes or help investigations, weakening police protection for the wider public.

nodes.title: More cover for criminals posing as agents
nodes.claim_html: More immigration enforcement paid for by S.2 would give criminals pretending to be immigration agents at least somewhat more opportunity to commit robberies, kidnappings and assaults.

nodes.title: Personal Security: injury, assault and lost police protection
nodes.claim_html: Violent encounters with agents during work and travel, weaker crime reporting that helps police stop dangerous offenders, and more cover for criminals posing as agents each threaten personal safety. Avoiding danger gives a reason against adding to them. Each needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: Less care available at home, in nursing homes and hospitals
nodes.claim_html: The added removals would reduce the supply of care workers enough that at least some Americans needing care at home, in nursing homes or in hospitals get less of it.

nodes.title: Fear keeps people from care and delays finding infections
nodes.claim_html: The added enforcement would lead at least some more people to delay or avoid health care, including vaccinations, delaying the identification and treatment of infectious disease in the community.

nodes.title: Infections spread from detention to the public
nodes.claim_html: The added detention would increase the chance that infections spreading in detention reach the wider public, for example through staff who move between facility and community.

nodes.title: Fear and mental-health harm for an average American
nodes.claim_html: The added enforcement operations would expose an average American, not only people facing enforcement, to fear or trauma that harms mental health.

nodes.title: Personal Security: health and access to care
nodes.claim_html: Being held without needed care, less care available when needed, delayed detection of infectious disease, infections spreading from detention, and fear that harms mental health each threaten personal health. Protecting health gives a reason against adding to them. Each needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: A steadier, ready security workforce
nodes.claim_html: Money that lasts across budget years, pays officers and covers unexpected costs would keep at least some trained Border Patrol and ICE officers paid and ready who might otherwise not be.

nodes.title: More detection of crossings and smuggling at the borders
nodes.claim_html: S.2’s border surveillance technology and tested autonomous towers would add at least some detection of unlawful crossings and smuggling that leads to interception.

nodes.title: Faster, safer response at land and sea borders
nodes.claim_html: S.2’s new aircraft and boats would make at least some responses to detected crossings, smuggling and other urgent situations at the borders faster or safer for officers.

nodes.title: Wider or better identity and departure checks
nodes.claim_html: S.2’s biometric entry and exit money would make identity and departure checks wider or more reliable, so false identities are harder to use.

nodes.title: Societal Security: control of the borders and a ready workforce
nodes.claim_html: A steadier, ready security workforce, more detection of crossings and smuggling, faster or safer response at land and sea borders, and harder-to-avoid identity checks each strengthen the state’s control of its borders and its ability to defend people. Each needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: More criminal money seized
nodes.claim_html: That added HSI time would reach financial investigations and lead to at least some more seizures of criminal networks’ money.

nodes.title: Added HSI time against unsafe equipment fraud
nodes.claim_html: That added HSI time would reach investigations of unsafe equipment sold to the military and police, as work outside the excluded customs mission.

nodes.title: Added HSI officers for major-event protection
nodes.claim_html: That added HSI time would add officers available to protect major public events and government gatherings.

nodes.title: Societal Security: protection against crime, terrorism and emergencies
nodes.claim_html: Usable drug inspections, less violence from people with violent convictions, more investigative work against terrorists, violent gangs, traffickers, scammers, cyberattackers and suppliers of unsafe military equipment, more abused children rescued, more criminal money seized, more officers available for major events, and more rescues or other emergency help each strengthen the state’s protection of people against threats. Each needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: Investigators pulled from other serious threats
nodes.claim_html: S.2’s immigration enforcement money would keep or increase the assignment of investigators away from serious crime and national security cases, leaving those threats less fully covered.

nodes.title: Fear keeps people from work, school and community life
nodes.claim_html: The added enforcement would lead at least some people to avoid work, school and community life out of fear, making towns less able to function.

nodes.title: Weaker essential services as workers are removed
nodes.claim_html: The added removals would take at least some workers who supply care, food and shelter, such as health, farm and construction workers, weakening those essential services.

nodes.title: A smaller national economy and public finances
nodes.claim_html: The added removals would shrink national production and tax money enough to reduce, at least somewhat, the country’s means to pay for protection and handle shocks.

nodes.title: Added debt pressure on defense and emergencies
nodes.claim_html: S.2’s added borrowing and interest costs would add at least somewhat to the money pressures on future decisions about defense and emergencies.

nodes.title: Societal Security: citizen protection and crime control
nodes.claim_html: Excessive force in public operations, less yearly leverage for Congress to demand safer conduct, weaker crime reporting, more cover for fake agents, investigators pulled from serious threats, and intimidation of people who watch officials each weaken the state’s protection of its citizens. Each needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: Societal Security: stable communities, services and finances
nodes.claim_html: Added community disruption from large raids, fear that keeps people from work, school and community life, weaker essential services, a smaller national economy and public finances, weaker defenses against disease, strained local water and sewer systems, and added debt pressure on defense and emergencies each threaten the stability a secure country depends on. Each needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: Less opioid abuse separating children from parents
nodes.claim_html: The lower drug supply would reduce, at least somewhat, opioid abuse that separates children from addicted parents.

nodes.title: Tradition: protecting the family setting where parents pass on faith
nodes.claim_html: Less opioid abuse separating children from addicted parents protects the family setting in which parents teach their children faith.

nodes.title: Tradition: family unity and parents passing on faith
nodes.claim_html: Separating children from parents disrupts shared family life and the daily example through which parents pass on faith, a family duty that the tradition treats as foundational.

nodes.title: Fear keeps more Christians from shared worship and rites
nodes.claim_html: The added enforcement would keep at least some more Christians away from shared worship, teaching and church rites out of fear, beyond what enforcement under the law in force already does.

nodes.title: Removals put congregations’ continuity at risk
nodes.claim_html: The added removals would take at least some pastors or enough members from congregations to put their continuity as communities of worship and teaching at risk.

nodes.title: More interruptions of established church ministries
nodes.claim_html: The added enforcement operations would raise the risk of further interruptions to established church ministries such as this church’s food ministry.

nodes.title: More Christians held where clergy cannot visit
nodes.claim_html: The added custody would hold at least some more Christians in places where pastors cannot get in to pray with them and give pastoral care.

nodes.title: Tradition: the church’s shared worship, community, ministry and pastoral care
nodes.claim_html: Fear that keeps people from shared worship and rites, the loss of congregations’ pastors or members, interrupted church ministries, and custody where clergy cannot visit each weaken the established church practices through which Christian teaching and customs continue. Each needs its own claim; any one accepted claim is enough.

nodes.title: More Christians returned to religious persecution
nodes.claim_html: The added removal money would return at least some more Christians, or relatives who go with them, to countries where they face religious persecution, despite the legal bar on such removals.

nodes.title: Tradition: Christians’ freedom to live by their faith
nodes.claim_html: Returning Christians and their relatives to countries that persecute them takes away their freedom to worship and live by their faith, which the tradition commits its members to defend.

value_subjects.S2_V_UNC_ABROAD: more perpetrators of human-rights violations and war crimes held responsible
value_subjects.S2_V_UNC_LIVES: fewer drugs reaching people, more rescues, or more medical care in custody (any one is enough)
value_subjects.S2_V_UNC_CAMERAS: more recorded encounters available to review how officers treat people
value_subjects.S2_V_UNC_WORKERS: safer work for agency staff through protective equipment or training
value_subjects.S2_V_UNC_FREEDOM: more custody of people who pose no safety threat, or an arrest fund that cannot pay for monitored release (either is enough)

value_subjects.S2_V_UNT_PERSECUTION: more persecutors held responsible, or more investigative work against foreign threats to critics (any one is enough)

value_subjects.S2_V_UNT_GROUPS: more stops based on perceived background, or more detention that blocks minority worship (either is enough)
value_subjects.S2_V_UNT_NEIGHBORS: more removals of established neighbors who are not threats, or an arrest fund that cannot pay for monitored release (either is enough)
value_subjects.S2_V_UNT_LISTEN: more Latino residents withdrawing from police contact and community life
